Items.Authors: Hannah C. Gulick, Shunsaku Nagasawa, Koothodil Abhijith Augustine, Melodi Ebrahimi, Mathew Dexter, Josh Forgione, Hannah Goldberg, Nihal Gulati, Sarah Jauregui, Andrew Ji, Chris Moeckel, Aldo Aguilar-Nadalini, Kazuhiro Nakazawa, Keigo Okuma, Srisha Rewatkar, Isabel Schmidtke, Andreas Zoglauer, Tadayuki Takahashi, Juan Carlos Martinez Oliveros, John Tomsick
Items.Title: Ground calibration of the Background and Transient Observer (BTO) gamma-ray instrument on COSI
Items.Abstract: The Background and Transient Observer (BTO) is a soft gamma-ray instrument that will fly on NASA’s Compton Spectrometer and Imager (COSI) mission in 2027. BTO is a Student Collaboration project that consists of two NaI(Tl) detectors, SiPM readouts, and custom electronics, providing spectra and light curves in the 30 keV to 2 MeV range. BTO has two primary science goals: detect astrophysical transients and monitor the soft gamma-ray background.     In this talk, I will present the comprehensive ground calibration campaign undertaken to prepare BTO for flight, including system characterization and environmental qualification. The results from these tests verify instrument robustness and characterize the expected on-orbit performance. Finally, I will discuss how the calibration results map onto BTO’s science capabilities, including transient sensitivity, background modeling accuracy, and expected on-orbit performance within the COSI mission.

Items.Authors: Corentin Cudennec, Alexandre Jeanneau, Roland Bacon, Thierry Lépine, Matthew Lehnert, Rémi Giroud, Jean-Emmanuel Migniau, David Lee, Roelof S. de Jong, Laurane Fréour
Items.Title: Guiding design choices for wide-field IFS: trade-off between replication and complexity for WST
Items.Abstract: The Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope (WST) is a proposed 12-meter segmented telescope optimized for seeing-limited observations in the visible. It is designed for the simultaneous operation of a high-multiplex multi-object spectrograph (30,000 fibers) and a large panoramic integral field spectrograph (3×3 arcmin). This paper presents the integrated design approach adopted for the IFS, focusing on a trade study of spectrograph architectures. We explore design choices such as pixel pitch, detector format, and camera optical design against throughput, image quality, error budgets, volume, cost, and image slicer geometry. The study adds one ecological metric: the CO₂ footprint of building each spectrograph, to inform design sustainability. The study also explores the potential of curved detectors, which can improve aberration control and throughput. Early results suggest that many simpler spectrographs outperform fewer complex units technically and economically.

Items.Authors: Haowen Li, Tao You, Jueqi Lin, Zheng Wang
Items.Title: Hardware/software architecture for the active surface control system of a 3m single-dish submillimeter telescope
Items.Abstract: We present a hardware/software architecture for the active surface control system of a 3m single-dish submillimeter telescope. This system actively corrects the primary reflector’s surface to compensate for the deformations caused by gravity, thermal effects, structural imperfections, and other factors. The hardware integrates high-precision temperature sensors with a control system that regulates the thermoelectric cooler (TEC) modules installed on steel rod standoffs, maintaining the reflector’s shape in response to deformations. The software provides data acquisition, advanced control algorithms, and visualization tools for continuous monitoring and real-time adjustment. The hardware and software constitute a practical, reliable, and scalable solution for preserving high surface accuracy and good beam performance for the telescope.

Items.Authors: Kjetil Dohlen, David Le Mignant, Timothy J. Morris, Marc Dubbeldam, David King, Deborah Malone, Lazar Staykov, Andrew Dunn, Iago Funes Vecino, Johan Floriot, Zalpha Challita, Jean-François Sauvage, Laurent Jocou, Alexis Carlotti, Anne Bonnefoi, Anne Costille, Teodora Aleida Viera-Curbelo
Items.Title: HARMONI at ELT: reoptimising the natural guide star sensors (NGSS) system for MCAO compatibility
Items.Abstract: HARMONI is the first light, adaptive optics assisted, near-IR integral field spectrograph for the ELT. It covers a spectral range from below 800nm to 2450nm with resolving powers from 3000 to 7000 and spatial sampling of 25mas and 6mas. This paper describes the impact on the natural guide star sensors (NGSS) system of the rescope of the instrument involving going behind the MORFEO MCAO system, Wide-ranging changes have been imposed in particular to the low-order wavefront sensors (LOWFS) previously optimized for LTAO operation, as well as on the external support and enclosure (ESE) whose external interfaces have changed. The high-contrast module (HCM) is also deeply affected due to the modified plate scale of the instrument, and the single-conjucate AO sensor (SCAOS) benefits from a reduced patrol field requirement

Items.Authors: Victor Mauger-Vauglin, Jean-Emmanuel Migniau, Matthieu Guibert, Magali Loupias, Eric Daguisé, Alban Remillieux
Items.Title: HARMONI at ELT: update and numerical simulation of a cryostat for HARMONI AIT
Items.Abstract: HARMONI is the first light, adaptive optics assisted, near-IR integral field spectrograph for the ELT. It covers a spectral range from 800nm to 2450nm with resolving powers from 3000 to 7000 and spatial sampling of 25mas and 6mas. It can operate in two adaptive optics modes - SCAO (including a high contrast capability) and MCAO. The project is resuming its final design phase after a rescope design phase in 2025.  The Integral Field Unit (IFU) sub-system is part of an Integral Field Spectrograph cooled down to 130K. The IFU is in charge of splitting, slicing and rearranging the field of view into four long slits (~540mm) to feed four spectrographs. The alignment of each of the subsystems will be tested at 130K with our test cryostat upgraded to fit with the alignment control tools. This paper presents the thermal simulation of the current cryostat, fed by real tests data, in order to better estimate the thermal behaviour foreseen after its upgrade.

Items.Authors: C. Guillermo Gimenez de Castro, Carlos Francile, Fernando M. López, Tiago Giorgetti, Paulo J. Simões, Amauri S. Kudaka, Daniel R. de Sousa, Manuel G. Marciani, Gedeane G. Kenshima
Items.Title: HATS: a mid-IR photometer to investigate solar flares
Items.Abstract: We present the first mid-IR solar dedicated telescope to detect flares at the almost unexplored wavelength λ = 20 μm or 15 THz. The High Altitude THz Solar photometer (HATS) uses a thermally stabilized Golay cell as a detector and a bandpass filter to select the observing frequency. It is installed at 2350 m above sea level in the Andes Mountains (Argentina). HATS started the commissioning phase in April 2025. The main goal of the instrument is to comprehend the physical processes that occur during flares at chromospheric levels. HATS is part of several other instruments operated at CRAAM to observe solar flares at the IR to submillimeter wavelength range.

Items.Authors: Dan A. Kerley, Malcolm Smith, Edward Chapin, Jonathan Stocks, Lianne Mueller, Colin Richardson, Jean-Pierre Véran, Maaike van Kooten, Kate Jackson
Items.Title: HEART in action: supporting RTC development across many AO instruments and observatories
Items.Abstract: The Herzberg Extensible Adaptive Optics Real-time Toolkit (HEART) is a versatile software framework designed to support the development of AO RTCs. Developed by the National Research Council Canada - Herzberg Astronomy and Astrophysics Research Centre (NRC-HAA), HEART provides a modular collection of utilities and components and a scalable framework that enable efficient construction of RTCs across diverse AO systems. It is currently being used to build or design RTCs for several major AO system such as MORFEO and ANDES for ELT; GNAO, GPI2 and GIRMOS for Gemini; and NFIRAOS for TMT. HEART is also deployed on-sky in REVOLT at DAO. This paper highlights how HEART enables the construction of these distinct RTCs by reducing the need for extensive customization, while leveraging reusable components to enhance robustness, scalability, and development efficiency.

Items.Authors: Peter G. Tuthill
Items.Title: Here be dragons: interferometry and the inception of the Wolf-Rayet Pinwheels
Items.Abstract: A quarter century has passed since optical interferometry delivered the first resolved images of elegant structures spun by entangled winds surrounding colliding-wind Wolf-Rayet binary stars. These dusty expanding spirals heralded a species new to astrophysical taxonomy: the WR Pinwheel nebulae. Encoding a wealth of key astrophysics of stellar winds and mass loss, community interest in these pinwheels snowballed, exploiting techniques from the millimetre to the x-ray. Although formed by seemingly simple underlying physics, the dust is folded and layered into elaborately sculpted forms featuring nested concentric shells creating some of the most arresting and popular public images yet produced by JWST. This paper charts the journey from discovery through to the present understanding of these exotic systems, highlighting the critical role played by optical interferometry in revealing the physical interplay of orbit, wind and shock written in the folds and coils of the intricate plumes.

Items.Authors: Masato Kagitani, Keisuke Takahashi, Ryo Tsukui, Mikio Kurita, Yasuhiro Hirahara, Takeshi Sakanoi, Marcelo Emilio, Simone Daflon, Kevin Lewis
Items.Title: High dynamic-range observation using a 1.8-m off-axis telescope PLANETS: primary mirror polish and its support structures
Items.Abstract: The PLANETS telescope is a 1.8-m off-axis system using contrast-enhancement techniques to observe faint emissions near bright sources. The primary mirror is an off-axis parabola (CLEARCERAM, D = 1850 mm, f = 4333 mm, off-axis distance 1800 mm). We completed the final polishing with LogistLab Inc. using a unique “dragging three-probe method.” Three laser probes measure curvature along straight paths, and the figure is reconstructed by second-order integration. Multiple intersecting and circular scans provide <20 nm RMS accuracy. The system is robust against vibration and temperature changes, and a robotic arm enables rapid switching between metrology and polishing. The primary mirror (510 kg, 100 mm edge thickness) is supported by 36 active back supports and 24 active lateral supports: a whiffletree with active warping harnesses for the back, and a Schwesinger-compliant design with harnesses for the side. We will report the latest metrology and on-site Hartmann test results.

Items.Authors: Hitesh Gajjar
Items.Title: High precision fabrication techniques for SALT integral field units
Items.Abstract: The development of the Integral Field Unit (IFU) for the Southern African Large Telescope (SALT) represents a significant advancement in the precision engineering and optical instrumentation capabilities of the South African Astronomical Observatory (SAAO). The IFU is designed to enable simultaneous spatial and spectral data acquisition, substantially enhancing the telescope’s scientific productivity across a wide range of astrophysical applications.    This paper presents the high-precision fabrication, assembly, and testing processes undertaken in the development of the SALT IFU. Particular attention is given to the manufacturing tolerances required to achieve optimal optical alignment and throughput efficiency, as well as to the metrology and quality-control techniques employed throughout production. The integration of advanced micro-fabrication methods, custom fibre positioning, and mechanical stability design are discussed in detail.

Items.Authors: Alexander Yavorsky, Barak Zackay
Items.Title: High-contrast imaging by phase gradient statistics in the Fourier domain
Items.Abstract: We present a statistical high-contrast imaging technique based on the reconstruction of speckle patterns from  series of short-exposure images. The method operates in the Fourier domain and analyzes the gradient of its phase, which is a continuous and well-defined quantity with a zero mean. To maximize the detection contrast, we account for the conditional variance of the gradients depending on the complex amplitude of the Fourier-transformed image and weight the gradients accordingly. We also implement an ADI-like technique to combine information from several color channels. Using QWSSI on the 4.3 m Lowell Discovery Telescope (LDT), we reach detection contrast of 10 mag at 0.5 arcseconds and 7.5 mag at 0.1 arcsecond angular separation on a real V = 3 spectroscopic binary with 1 ms exposure time and only 18 seconds integration time.

Items.Authors: Lorenzo Cabona, Riccardo Claudi, Gianluca Galzerano, Francesco Canella, Alessio Gambetta, Niccolò Barberio, Riccardo Ciantini, Stefania Stefani, Paolo Laporta
Items.Title: High-Precision NIR absorption gas cell characterization for GIANO-B via broadband GHz dual-comb spectroscopy
Items.Abstract: We present the filling procedure and the subsequent characterization of the two absorption gas cells (H and K bands) designed to enable high-precision wavelength calibration for GIANO-B spectrograph. The characterization of the reference cells was performed using dual-comb spectroscopy. Recent advances in GHz-repetition-rate optical frequency combs have enabled fast, broadband measurements, while software-based phase-noise compensation strategies have recently improved SNR performance when operating free-running combs. We measure the spectral features in the 1000–2400 nm range, with a spectral resolution of 1 GHz. The experiment uses two identical mode-locked lasers operating at ~1 GHz repetition rate, with a relative repetition-rate offset. The laser pulses are amplified, compressed, and spectrally broadened in new-generation Ta₂O₅ waveguides. Accurate wavelength referencing is provided by beating the comb with a narrow-linewidth CW laser in combination with an absolute wavemeter.

Items.Authors: Bryson L. Cale, Jean-Baptiste Ruffio, Max Brodheim, Ava DeLaGarza, Graham Bruce Berriman, Jeff Mader, Charlie Kilpatrick, Don Neill, Samuel Halverson, Ben Sappey, Luke Finnerty, Quinn Konopacky, Ashley Baker, Charles Beichman, Rob Bertz, Jocelyn Ferrara, Michael P. Fitzgerald, Aidan Gibbs, Rose Gibson, Katelyn Horstman, Nemanja Jovanovic, Marc Kassis, Stephanie Leifer, Andrea Lin, Dimitri Mawet, Jason Wang
Items.Title: HISPEC data reduction pipeline I: Architecture and calibration data management
Items.Abstract: We present the design of the Data Reduction Pipeline (DRP) for the upcoming HISPEC instrument at W. M. Keck Observatory which performs the science and calibration processing for HISPEC. The HISPEC DRP uses a modular object-oriented programing (OOP) structure where individual DRP steps, pipelines, and data model classes are straightforward to implement and configure. A key component of the DRP is an automated calibration file association and retrieval system. Calibration metadata are stored in a local SQLite database that is synced with a PostgreSQL database hosted at the Keck Observatory Archive (KOA). Calibration files are automatically associated and downloaded from KOA and cached locally for efficient reuse. The design of the HISPEC DRP and automated calibration system minimizes user-intervention and provides a robust, reproducible environment for processing and analyzing HISPEC data products.

Items.Authors: Oscar Gonzalez, Martin Black, Stephen Watson, Matteo Munari, Andrea Tozzi, Marco Riva, Sofia Randich, Andrea Bianco, Letizia Caito
Items.Title: HRMOS: a novel concept for a fibre positioner system with integrated ADC
Items.Abstract: HRMOS is a very high-resolution (R~80,000), multi-object (50-60) spectrograph, proposed as a new instrument for the VLT. HRMOS will address a broad range of transformative science questions. To achieve its science goals, one of the key technical challenges is that of atmospheric dispersion correction over the 25’ field of view of the VLT. One of the concepts being explored is to achieve this correction in the focal plane fibre positioning system, reducing the need for very large ADC opto-mechanics. In this paper, we present a novel concept for a traditional pick-and-place system (named QUACKS) that utilises configurable pick-off mirror units that are oriented prior to placement (named DUCKS). The ADC is done using optical receiver units placed around the edge of the telescope field (named ROCKS). The current opto-mechanical design of the developing concept, which can also be used by other future facilities, will be presented together with an overview of its benefits and challenges.

Items.Authors: Anna Brucalassi, Andrea Tozzi, Matteo Munari, Andrea Bianco, Simone D'Auria, Jose Schiappacasse Ulloa, José A. Araiza-Durán, Alen Khanbekyan, Manuela Arnò, Andrea Baruffolo, Martin Black, Emma Fernandez-Alvar, Michele Frangiamore, Oscar A. Gonzalez, Robert J. Harris, Enrique Jovén Álvarez, Graham J. Murray, Luis Rodríguez Ramos, Bernardo Salasnich, Letizia Caito, Enrico Giro, Laura Magrini, Maria Sofia Randich, Marco Riva, Sergio Sousa
Items.Title: HRMOS: towards the spectrograph design
Items.Abstract: The High-Resolution Multi-Object Spectrograph (HRMOS) is a facility instrument that we plan to propose for the Very Large Telescope (VLT) of the European Southern Observatory (ESO). HRMOS offers a combination of capabilities that are crucial for enabling breakthrough science across a wide range of active research fields, including stellar astrophysics, exoplanet studies, and Galactic and Local Group archaeology. It addresses a significant gap in the suite of instruments planned for the coming decade. The key features of HRMOS include high spectral resolution (R~80,000), multi-object capability (50-80 targets), and long-term stability, enabling considerable radial-velocity precision and accuracy (10 m/s). In this work, we present the ongoing development of the opto-mechanical design for a next-generation high-resolution spectrograph, with a focus on key engineering solutions implemented to fulfill the instrument demanding scientific requirements.

Items.Authors: Emiel H. Por, Mayra Gutierrez, Dan Sirbu, Rachel Morgan, Eduardo Bendek, Carson Valdez, Kevin Fogarty, Jordan Diaz, Laurent Pueyo
Items.Title: Hybrid photonic coronagraphy: integration and testing on the SEAL testbed
Items.Abstract: Photonic integrated circuits (PICs) can act as coronagraphs by routing telescope light through Mach–Zehnder interfermeter meshes whose phase shifters direct starlight away from the nulled channels. However, imperfections in the PIC limit performance. We investigate hybrid photonic coronagraphs that place a bulk-optic coronagraph upstream, suppressing most starlight before injection and substantially relaxing PIC tolerance requirements.    We test this concept by integrating a NASA Ames AstroPIC device into the UCSC SEAL testbed, performing free-space injection of focal-plane light using a microlens array aligned to on-chip grating couplers . We outline the prototype’s optical, mechanical, and thermal design and report initial throughput, contrast, and stability measurements, comparing direct and hybrid injection. These results probe the feasibility of hybrid photonic coronagraphy for next-generation high-contrast imagers for both ground- and space-based telescopes.

Items.Authors: Miguel Angel Gonzalez Bolivar, David Clarke, Nuria P. F. Lorente, Nuwanthika Fernando
Items.Title: ImageNinja: a python framework for modular data simulations.
Items.Abstract: We created ImageNinja, a framework designed to build modular raw data simulations. Each simulation is driven by a series Python classes called Effectors. Each Effector replicates an aspect in the instrument’s data-generation process, from detector characteristics and external noise, to writing the raw data to FITS files. ImageNinja is designed to be instrument-agnostic, but its development has been focused on a specific instrument: the MCAO Assisted Visible Imager and Spectrograph (MAVIS). The current version of ImageNinja consists of three packages: CORE, FITS, and MAVIS. ImageNinja-CORE implements the main simulation framework, allowing users to plug in modules that perform the simulation steps. ImageNinja-FITS provides Effectors for the I/O of FITS files. Finally, ImageNinja-MAVIS contains the Effectors that replicate the data-collection process specific to MAVIS.

Items.Authors: Francesco Ceraudo, Giovanni Della Casa, Matias Antonelli, Giuseppe Bertuccio, Riccardo Campana, Ettore Del Monte, Evgeny Demenev, Yuri Evangelista, Marco Feroci, Francesco Ficorella, Mauro Fiorini, Edoardo Giancarli, Jacopo Giani, Marco Grassi, Giovanni Lombardi, Piero Malcovati, Filippo Mele, Alessio Nuti, Giancarlo Pepponi, Alexander Rachevski, Irina Rashevskaya, Ajay Sharma, Marco Tambussi, Gianluigi Zampa, Nicola Zampa, Yinhe Zhu, Nicola Zorzi, Francesca Esposito, Immacolata Donnarumma, Alessandro Turchi, Ugo Cortesi, Fabio D'Amico, Marco Gai, Andrea Argan
Items.Title: Imaging and spectroscopic performances of the detector assemblies for the lunar electromagnetic monitor in X-rays
Items.Abstract: The Lunar Electromagnetic Monitor in X-rays (LEM-X) is an Italian proposal for a Moon-based all-sky X-ray observatory, for the detection of transients and the long-term monitoring of sources in the 2-50 keV band, developed within the Earth Moon Mars project of the Italian National Recovery and Resilience Plan. Featuring a modular design, LEM-X is based on compact and lightweight coded-aperture cameras, each with a 2-sr field of view. The detector plane of each camera is built around four alumina-based Detector Assemblies (DAs), each one featuring a large-area (~7x7 cm2) Silicon Drift Detector (SDD), readout by CMOS analog Application Specific Integrated Circuits (AFE ASICs) named NOVA and specifically developed for this project. Four complete DAs, i.e. the full detector plane of one LEM-X caamera were developed and assembled. We will present the results of the performance tests demonstrating both the spectral and imaging capabilities of the devices.

Items.Authors: Paul Rouquette, Benoît Neichel, Taissir Héritier, Pierre Jouve, Anne Costille, Kjetil Dohlen, Thierry Fusco
Items.Title: Impact of microlenses shape on the performance of the ELT laser guide star sensor
Items.Abstract: In this paper, the impact of the Shack-Hartmann microlenses on adaptive optics performances is characterized. To this end, an original approach combining microlens profile measurements, end-to-end simulations and experimental validation is proposed.

Items.Authors: Davide Savio
Items.Title: Impact of modal noise on absolute wavelength calibration with fiber-fed laser frequency combs
Items.Abstract: Modal noise arising from fiber coupling can limit the accuracy of Laser Frequency Comb calibration in high-resolution spectrometers. We present experimental evidence showing how non-uniform fiber illumination leads to systematic wavelength distortions in individual calibration lines, in particular when classical scrambling techniques such as double scramblers and octagonal fibers are used. While the impact on traditional radial velocity measurements, based on the average of many spectral lines, remains negligible, single-line wavelength determinations can be affected at the level of many meters per second. These effects are particularly relevant for experiments that require accurate line-by-line wavelength comparisons, such as the search for possible variations of fundamental constants over cosmological timescales. Understanding and mitigating modal noise is therefore essential for next-generation high-accuracy spectrographs.

Items.Authors: Hanindyo Kuncarayakti, Hele I. Savin, Gregory Bredthauer, Oskari Leiviskä, Seppo Mattila, Olli Setälä, Joseph Tufts, Ville Vähänissi, Petri Väisänen, Joonas Viuho
Items.Title: Implementation of black silicon CCD for astronomical observations at the Nordic Optical Telescope
Items.Abstract: Nano-structured, or so-called "black" silicon detectors can attain higher quantum efficiency and wider wavelength sensitivity range compared to traditional silicon CCDs and CMOS sensors. These qualities are attractive for applications in low-light conditions such as in astronomical observations. We present the first concept of an instrument employing a black silicon CCD detector, planned to be mounted and tested at the Nordic Optical Telescope in the Canary Islands, Spain. In this presentation, the preliminary design of the instrument and the plan of the implementation of the black silicon CCD chip in the instrument will be described. Characterization and test plans for the instrument in both sea-level laboratory and mountaintop on-site conditions will be discussed, followed by the utilization strategy of the instrument in actual astronomical observations.

Items.Authors: Haruka Suzuki, Itsuki Sakon, Takashi Onaka, Aoi Takahashi, Takafumi Ootsubo, Naofumi Fujishiro, Youichi Ohyama, Hideo Matsuhara
Items.Title: Improved data reduction procedure for the mid-infrared slit spectroscopy of AKARI/IRC LG2
Items.Abstract: In this presentation, we report on our technical efforts to evaluate and mitigate artifacts that have hindered accurate spectral extraction in AKARI Infrared Camera (IRC) LG2 slit spectroscopy. The AKARI/IRC LG2 slit spectroscopic data suffer from artifacts such as contamination by zeroth- and second-order light in the edge regions of the aperture mask, as well as scattered light produced by the incident beam within the field of view.    To establish a standardized procedure for deriving reliable LG2 slit spectra, we investigate the efficiencies of the zeroth-, first-, and second-order light, the slit properties, the geometry of the aperture mask, and the characteristics of the scattered light. Through these analyses, we develop a robust data-reduction method that eliminates previously uncorrected artifacts and enables accurate extraction of LG2 slit spectra, particularly for diffuse sources.

Items.Authors: Christopher Foster, Charles White, Kevin Kady, Christian Guerra, Christopher Sanchez
Items.Title: Improvements of the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope facility thermal systems control software
Items.Abstract: The controls of the U.S. National Science Foundations’s (NSF) Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST) Facility Management System (FMS) have evolved with continuous improvement based upon the needs over the telescope’s evolution. The FMS is the system that controls the thermal operations. The FMS controls have evolved and changed as the needs of the telescope have changed and as lessons were learned. As the telescope moved from operational commissioning to operations, there was an opportunity to engage an outside consulting firm to engage in a thorough review of the entire thermal system both to gain perspective on the overall design as well as to check for potential energy savings and improved operations. The engineering firm Burns & McDonnell was hired to work with involved DKIST employees to perform this review. This paper is a review of the lessons learned during commissioning of the FMS as well as the results and recommendations from the consultation.

Items.Authors: Alex Thomas, Bugao Zou, Yuhan Wang, Erin Healy, Shreya Sutariya, Claire Lessler, Jeffrey McMahon, Michael Niemack
Items.Title: Infrared blocking foam filters for millimeter-wave cameras
Items.Abstract: As the mechanisms governing the attenuation of IR-blocking foams used in Cosmic Microwave Background experiments were poorly understood, we present broadband (150 GHz to 1.5 THz) transmission spectroscopy of these foams, including Zotefoams (BICEP/Keck, SPT, CCAT, SO LAT) and Styroace-II (POLARBEAR, SO SATs). Our data are fit with a radiative transfer model incorporating Rayleigh scattering, Mie scattering, dielectric absorption, and higher-order scattering terms. We find that Zotefoams offer superior in-band transmission for mm and sub-mm bands. We also evaluate the tradeoff between Zotefoams, with lower densities offering increased transmission and decreased out-of-band attenuation. Finally, we estimate the scattering kernel and, therefore, the detector loading from blackbody radiation scattered at wide angles. In combination with our study of capacitive metal-mesh filters, we present quantitative recommendations for IR blocking filters for mm and sub-mm-wave observations.

Items.Authors: Fabio Muleri, Luca Baldini, Sudip Chakraborty, Chien-Ting Chen, Enrico Costa, Ettore Del Monte, Alessandro Di Marco, Kurtis L. Dietz, Sergio Fabiani, Riccardo Ferrazzoli, Philip Kaaret, Alberto Manfreda, Stephen L. O'Dell, John Rankin, Brian D. Ramsey, Carmelo Sgrò, Paolo Soffitta, Douglas A. Swartz, Allyn F. Tennant, Alessio Trois, Martin C. Weisskopf
Items.Title: In-orbit anomaly and recovery of IXPE detector 2
Items.Abstract: The Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE) is a NASA-ASI mission launched in December 2021 and dedicated to the measurement of linear polarization in the X-ray energy range, between 2 and 8 keV. The payload is comprised of three identical telescopes, with grazing-incidence mirrors focusing radiation on focal plane photoelectric polarimeters based on the Gas Pixel Detector design. On 14 April 2025, the second detector had an anomaly that changed significantly the electrical behaviour of the ASIC which reads out the image of the photoelectron tracks. In this contribution, we describe the effect of the anomaly on the instrumental response and the actions taken to mitigate its effects and recover the scientific observations of the instrument.

Items.Authors: Jean-Paul Breuer, Masato Yokota, Yasushi Fukazawa, Hiromitsu Takahashi, Jakub Řı́pa, Mariana Dafčíková, Filip Münz, Norbert Werner, Masanori Ohno, Balázs Csák, László Mészáros, András Pál, Marcel Frajt, Ján Hudec, Jakub Kapuš, Maksim Rezenov, Vladimír Dániel, Juraj Dudáš, Petr Svoboda, Hsiang-Kuang Chang, Chin-Ping Hu, Chih-Hsun Lin, Tsung-Che Liu, Kaustubha Sen, Che-Chih Tsao, Chih-En Wu
Items.Title: Instrument response generation using high-resolution 3D voxilization of GRBAlpha and VZLUSat-2 satellites with MEGAlib
Items.Abstract: Pathfinder gamma-ray burst (GRB) detecting CubeSat missions such as GRBAlpha and VZLUSAT-2 have demonstrated the successful application of scintillator detectors with silicon photomultipliers in low Earth orbit (LEO). To produce more comprehensive scientific analysis of the data, the effective area of the detector needs to be characterised at different energies. A large part of this process requires a thorough understanding of the detectors response matrices as a function of the satellite mass model typically performed through Geant4 and MEGAlib simulations. We use a novel voxilization and binning methodology to turn complex 3D geometries into MEGAlib-compatible versions, and we validate these experiments by showing that the simulation results with Geant4 agree within an order of 10%. We use MEGAlib simulations from various angles around the spacecraft to generate instrumental response matrixes for both simple and complex geometries, in the case of GRBAlpha and VZLUSAT-2, respectively.

Items.Authors: Prakriti Gupta`, John I. Bailey, James D. Neill, Michael Langmayr
Items.Title: InstrumentKit - a framework generator for astronomical instruments
Items.Abstract: The development of new astronomical instruments often demands extensive research and effort in designing the Instrument Control System (ICS). A significant portion of time is spent selecting appropriate tools and integrating them into a cohesive framework. However, due to tight development schedules and competing priorities, software for the ICS is frequently deferred or implemented in a “good enough” state. As a result, end users and observatory operations must contend with suboptimal systems for years to come.     InstrumentKit aims to transform this landscape by providing a robust, modular framework for ICS development. It offers a structured software architecture and a curated, well-integrated stack of tools that accelerate development and improve long-term maintainability. Its modular design also ensures adaptability; allowing developers to incorporate evolving technologies and methodologies to support the next generation of astronomical instruments.

Items.Authors: Pietro Ferraiuolo, Marco Bonaglia, Enrico Pinna, Azzaroli Nicolò, Luca Carbonaro, Giulia Carlà, Tommaso Lapucci, Paolo Spanò, Raffaele Tomelleri, Giovanni Negrini, Cristian Morando, Fabio Rossi, Matteo Menessini, Simone Esposito
Items.Title: Integration and alignment of the Petalometer testbench at INAF-Arcetri
Items.Abstract: Accurate phasing of segmented adaptive mirrors is a key requirement for achieving diffraction-limited performance on ELTs. Within the STILES project (PNRR), the INAF–Arcetri Adaptive Optics group is developing a dedicated petalometer testbench to evaluate phasing sensors for the ELT’s M4 mirror and GMT's M2. The bench integrates a six-segment “petalmirror,” each petal offering a 12 µm piston stroke, with internal metrology which will allow to measure the segment's relative piston with respect to the fixed central segment with nanometer accuracy. After completing hardware procurement, the team finalized acceptance measurements of the petalmirror and is now integrating the metrology system and the main optical relay—composed of the source unit and off-axis parabolas. The testbench will provide a controlled environment for validating phasing strategies for future ELT-class adaptive mirrors.

Items.Authors: Monde Manzini, Katlego Papane, Vhulahani Manukha, Evelyn Nkgadima
Items.Title: Integration and test facility effect towards operational SKA‑Mid telescope: a systems engineering approach
Items.Abstract: The Square Kilometre Array Mid-Frequency Telescope (SKA-Mid) is a massive, complex radio telescope system. To manage risks from its scale and digital complexity—where minor errors can cascade—the project employs a rigorous Systems Engineering approach. Central to this is an Integration and Test Facility (ITF) that serves as a high-fidelity digital twin and test environment. Using a specialized Sky Simulator as part of a Test Environment (TEnv), the ITF enables continuous verification of subsystems and core scientific performance in a controlled setting before deployment. This proactive strategy prevents costly on-site failures, ensuring the array meets its requirements and achieves operational resilience during the lifetime of the SKA-MId telescope. This paper outlines a systems engineering approach yielding a positive effect, risk mitigation and cost effective impact of having an ITF as a verification platform towards a successful commissioning and operation of the SKA-Mid telescope.

Items.Authors: Andrea Lin, Ashley Baker, Dimitri Mawet, Garreth Ruane, Gautam Vasisht, Sam Halverson, Nemanja Jovanovic
Items.Title: Investigating the differential limb coupling effect for diffraction-limited spectrographs with PARVI
Items.Abstract: The upcoming HISPEC spectrograph for Keck II will use single-mode fibers fed by the telescope’s adaptive optics system, making it one of a handful of diffraction-limited spectrographs capable of precision radial velocities (PRVs). However, due to the target stars being partially resolved, the resulting RVs are predicted to be affected by differential limb coupling (DLC), where the red- and blue-shifted sides of the stellar disk are coupled unequally into the spectrograph across different epochs, producing an RV error term on the order of several m/s for nearby stars for HISPEC. We present our efforts to directly observe DLC on-sky for the first time with the diffraction-limited spectrograph PARVI in order to verify the expected behavior of DLC and subsequently develop mitigation strategies for HISPEC.

Items.Authors: Scott J. Lilley, Mahawa Cisse, Peter Wizinowich, Antonin Bouchez, Eduardo Marin, Jason Worden, Jacob Taylor, Charlotte Guthery, Ed Wetherell, Marc Kassis, Nemanja Jovanovic, Mitsuko Roberts, Philip Hinz, Dominic Sanchez
Items.Title: Keck AO near-infrared wavefront sensor (‘IWA): preliminary design
Items.Abstract: A new near-Infrared Wavefront sensor (‘IWA) is being developed to optimize the Keck II AO system’s performance for science with the recently installed High order Advanced Keck Adaptive optics (HAKA) deformable mirror (DM). ‘IWA will significantly enhance the performance and sky coverage delivered by the Keck II AO system to the existing ORKID imager and a suite of new science instruments: a mid-infrared coronagraphic integral field spectrograph (SCALES) and a fiber-fed high-resolution spectrograph (HISPEC).  We present the preliminary design of ‘IWA, focusing on the opto-mechanical design and the challenges of designing ‘IWA to fit within the limited space on the Keck II AO bench. We also present simulation results of the Keck II AO system’s performance with ‘IWA.

Items.Authors: Xiaojie Zhang, Haoran Yu, Jun Li, Yong Li, Cheng Liao, Yonghui Hou, Hangxin Ji
Items.Title: Key technologies for immersion systems in athermalized cameras of large optical telescopes: performance and stability evaluation of index matching fluids
Items.Abstract: This study evaluates the optical and physicochemical stability of Index Matching Fluids (IMFs) for immersion-based, athermalized cameras in large telescopes. We systematically characterized candidate fluids, identifying a key thermo-optic nonlinearity in high-index IMFs that constrains thermal management design. Material compatibility tests revealed incompatibilities for specific glasses and polymers, while confirming suitable inert alternatives. Accelerated aging further differentiated the long-term stability of various IMF formulations, with some showing risks of degradation. The results provide critical empirical data and practical guidelines for material selection and system design, directly supporting the development of reliable high-throughput immersion optics for next-generation astronomical instruments.

Items.Authors: Shutaro Ueda, Yasuhiro Shoji, Daisuke Yonetoku, Tatsuya Sawano, Makoto Arimoto, Shoya Matsuda, Yoshiyuki Ando, Ryota Heibatake, Kaito Ozawa, Kimiyoshi Ichikawa, Norio Tokuda
Items.Title: KSAT3-X01: a 3U-size CubeSat mission for exploring charged particles in the Earth's magnetosphere with diamond detectors
Items.Abstract: We present a concept of the KSAT3-X01 project led by Kanazawa University. KSAT3-X01 is a 3U-size CubeSat mission planning for launch in 2027, aiming to explore charged particles in the Earth's magnetosphere with diamond detectors developed by Kanazawa University. Observations of charged particles, including electrons, protons, and ions, in the Earth's magnetosphere have revealed that an amount of charged particles is escaped from the Earth's magnetosphere. However, mechanism(s) to accelerate such particles remains unclear. In addition, it is challenging to measure the population of lower-energy particles at a few 10 keV. To address these problems, we have been developing our diamond detectors onboard KSAT3-X01. We measure the X-ray spectroscopic performance of the diamond detectors to evaluate signal charge corrections inside the diamond with several radioisotopes such as 241Am, 133Ba, and 109Cd. We find that our diamond detectors can detect X-rays above at least 10 keV.

Items.Authors: Michele Frangiamore
Items.Title: Large size VPHGs@INAF: new facility and perspectives
Items.Abstract: Volume Phase Holographic (VPH) technology is crucial in modern ground-based astronomical spectrographs due to high diffraction efficiency, tunability, and robustness. At INAF–Astronomical Observatory of Brera, we focus on the design and fabrication of VPHGs for diverse instruments.    Next-generation facilities require large-format VPHGs, up to half a meter, for instruments such as MOSAIC (ELT), HRMOS (VLT), and WST, demanding scalable, precise production processes.    At INAF–OABr, we developed a reliable manufacturing process ensuring control of diffraction efficiency, wavefront quality, and dispersion. A new holography laboratory, with a 450 mm aperture writing setup, allows production of VPHGs up to 450×600 mm (vertical and dispersion directions, respectively).     Initial results demonstrate the capabilities and future potential for large-format gratings in advanced spectrographs.

Items.Authors: Swati Ravi, Alan Garner, Jill Juneau, Elio Angile, Ralf K. Heilmann, Herman Marshall, Sarah Heine, Beverly LaMarr, Sean McNeil, Stephen Bongiorno
Items.Title: Laser metrology for precision alignment of transmission gratings in the REDSoX soft X-ray polarimeter
Items.Abstract: Precise alignment of transmission gratings is critical for the Rocket Experiment Demonstration of a Soft X-ray Polarimeter (REDSoX), a NASA sounding-rocket mission delivering the first sub-1 keV X-ray spectro-polarimetry. The instrument's laterally graded multilayer mirrors require dispersed light to land on precise positions of the mirror, with angular errors of ~0.1° reducing modulation efficiency and spectral response. We apply a dual-beam laser metrology method that measures surface slope with a normal-incidence beam and first-order diffraction with an oblique beam, enabling sensitive, non-contact extraction of yaw, pitch, roll, and in-plane period variations. We report on adapting this technique to REDSoX geometry, tolerances, and flight-qualification needs. This approach provides rapid assessment of grating alignment and local distortions without repeated X-ray tests and offers a scalable, mission-agnostic framework for future spectroscopic and spectropolarimetric instruments.

Items.Authors: Nicola Brancadori, Enea Boria, Francesco Cavaliere, Cristian Franceschet, Elenia Manzan, Aniello Mennella, Filippo Montonati, Federico Pezzotta, Federico Bassi, Paolo de Bernardis, Marco Bersanelli, Alessandro Coppolecchia, Armando Favi, Enrico Gallus, Massimo Gervasi, Luca Lamagna, Silvia Masi, Alessandro Paiella, Andrea Passerini, Giorgio Pettinari, Francesco Piacentini, Elisabetta Tommasi, Angela Volpe, Mario Zannoni
Items.Title: Laser-micromachined aluminum platelets applied to high-frequency microwave passive components for CMB applications
Items.Abstract: This work presents an array of 77 corrugated feed horns coupled with 77 waveguide orthomode transducers (OMTs) operating in the 200–280 GHz range, fabricated from aluminum platelets using a high-precision laser micromachining process. This technique provides low cost, high repeatability, and excellent scalability, making it suitable for large focal planes required in CMB polarization experiments. The feed horns achieve typical CMB performance, with simulated cross-polarization ≤ −25 dB and sidelobes ≤ −30 dB, while the OMTs use a turnstile-junction design with simulated cross-polarization ≤ −60 dB. Metrological measurements show smooth surfaces (≈7 µm rms) and accurate feature reproduction (≈3 µm deviation), along with a systematic ≈25 µm shift of hole centers due to thermal stretching. Simulations indicate that this mainly increases cross-polarization to −20/−30 dB, still compatible with CMB requirements. These results are currently being validated through ongoing RF measurements.

Items.Authors: Jason E. Austermann, James Beall, Andrew Forsman, Haibo Huang, Johannes Hubmayr, Matthew Koc, Jeffrey van Lanen, Pavel Lapa, Joshua Raimist, Jordan Stutz, Anatolios Tambazidis, Joel Ullom
Items.Title: Laser-micromachined silicon platelet feedhorns for large-scale, submillimeter and millimeter-wave focal planes
Items.Abstract: We present the fabrication and characterization of the world’s first 150~mm diameter silicon platelet feedhorn array produced using laser micromachining. This feedhorn array is designed to operate in the submillimeter band centered at 350 GHz (330--370 GHz). We compare the performance of this array directly to those produced using traditional deep reactive-ion etching (DRIE), as well as to simulation. We present optical performance measurements at room-temperature and cryogenically coupled to KID detectors. In addition, we review and compare these results to a demonstration of laser-micromachined feedhorns designed for the millimeter-wave band of 80–160 GHz (i.e. typical CMB bands). Finally, we also present an exploration into additional advantages of laser-micromachining, including sidewall control and the potential of using thicker (and thus fewer) wafers, which could significantly reduce production costs and labor.

Items.Authors: Matteo Lombini, Michele Bellazzini, Emiliano Diolaiti, Fernando Pedichini, Andrea Baruffolo, Federico Battaini, Enrico Cascone, Fausto Cortecchia, Felice Cusano, Andrea Di Paola, Christian Eredia, Jacopo Farinato, Andrea Grazian, Diego Paris, Salvatore Savarese, Pietro Schipani, Laura Schreiber, Enzo Brocato, Roberto Gilli, Marco Mignoli, David E. Trilling, Fabio Vito, Dennis Zaritsky
Items.Title: LBCmos: extending wide-field imaging and photometry capabilities at LBTO to the next decades
Items.Abstract: LBCmos upgrades the Large Binocular Camera with new 8k × 8k sCMOS detectors, providing improved efficiency, fast readout, full-field coverage, and new narrow and medium-band filters. The redesign maintains the optical performance of LBC while modernizing mechanics, electronics, and software. Enhanced operational flexibility enables fast photometry and real-time diagnostics. LBCmos strengthens LBTO’s competitiveness in wide-field imaging and expands its scientific capabilities from stellar populations to high-redshift surveys.

Items.Authors: Nathan P. Magari, James E. Larkin, Shelley A. Wright, Bryson Cale, Michael P. Fitzgerald
Items.Title: Liger at W.M. Keck Observatory: lenslet IFS spectral extraction techniques
Items.Abstract: Liger is a next-generation imager and integral field spectrograph (IFS) currently being fabricated for the Keck I telescope. Liger will be delivered with a data reduction system (DRS) to produce science-quality images and IFS data cubes. In this paper we investigate advanced spectral extraction techniques for Liger’s lenslet mode. Using end-to-end simulations of the instrument optics and detector response, we optimize the spectral extraction algorithm based on accuracy, computational efficiency, and memory usage. In particular we explore a full 2-D convolution of the raw frame using a spectral point spread function (PSF) characterized by simulated arc lamp scans. We find that this procedure provides improved SNR in the reduced data cube compared to previous methods.

Items.Authors: Lawrence M. Machia
Items.Title: Lining it up: integrated focus and 4lt alignment systems for telescopes
Items.Abstract: The Argus Array is an 8-meter class, all-sky optical survey designed to discover transient events via sub-minute deep imaging. The instrument is comprised of 1200 individual telescopes and cameras which together observe the entire accessible sky simultaneously. The scale of the array presents an operational challenge for focusing and tilt-alignment in reasonable construction timescales. While off-the-shelf robotic focusers are relatively common, most instruments are manually tilt-aligned with shims. The number of telescopes in the Argus array precludes manual tilt-alignment. Here we present design and prototype of a custom Argus robotic alignment system which integrates focus and tilt-alignment capability into a single low-cost device.

Items.Authors: Anastasios Aretos, Younes Chahid, Chris Miller, Mark Cliffe, Graham Wilks, Lee Chapman
Items.Title: Liquid nitrogen pre-cooling system for ELT instruments utilising additively manufactured heat exchangers, integrated temperature and liquid level control
Items.Abstract: We propose an advanced alternative pre-cooling system architecture which uses additively manufactured heat exchangers with increased surface areas, embedded liquid level sensors as well as integrated heating elements, that provide tighter control over the pre-cooling process. We provide a comparison between the effects that the build material selection has to the manufacturing methods employed as well as the internal geometry of the heat exchanger. By using the incumbent pre-cooling system of HARMONI, as a base line we offer a comparison on the improvements that such a system offers over current and near future designs, both in cooling performance as well as system integration and overall manufacturing costs.

Items.Authors: Jakub Ripa, Filip Münz, Marianna Dafčíková, András Pál, Norbert Werner, Masanori Ohno, László Mészáros, Balázs Csák, Pavel Kosík, Michaela Ďuríšková, Lea Szakszonová, Martin Kolář, Tomáš Vítek, Nikola Husáriková, Filip Hroch, Michal Pazderka, Yasushi Fukazawa, Hiromitsu Takahashi, Tsunefumi Mizuno, Jean-Paul Breuer, Masato Yokota, Kazuhiro Nakazawa, Hirokazu Odaka, Yuto Ichinohe, Tomáš Urbanec, Aleš Povalač, Miroslav Kasal, Miroslav Šmelko, Peter Hanák, Gábor Galgóczi, Martin Topinka, Hsiang-Kuang Chang, Tsung-Che Liu, Chih-Hsun Lin, Chin-Ping Hu, Che-Chih Tsao, Kaustubha Sen, Chih-En Wu, Jakub Kapuš, Ján Hudec, Marcel Frajt, Maksim Rezenov, Vladimír Dániel, Petr Svoboda, Juraj Dudáš, Martin Sabol, Ivo Veřtát, Róbert László, Martin Koleda
Items.Title: Long-term performance of SiPMs in space environment measured by GRBAlpha, GRBBeta, and VZLUSAT-2 CubeSats
Items.Abstract: We report the successful application of silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) in gamma-ray burst detectors used in GRBAlpha, GRBBeta, and VZLUSAT-2 CubeSats operating in the low Earth orbit (LEO) radiation environment. We describe the changes in the dark count rate and low-energy threshold of S13360-3050 PE MPPCs by Hamamatsu, based on measurements spanning over four years. We have demonstrated that SiPMs, shielded by 2.5 mm of PbSb alloy, can be used in a LEO environment on a scientific mission lasting beyond four years. This shows the potential for SiPMs to be employed in future satellites.

Items.Authors: Matthew A. Koc, Jason Austermann, James Beall, Johannes Hubmayr, Joel N. Ullom, Michael Vissers, Jordan Wheeler
Items.Title: Low temperature performance of silicon micromachined waveguide filter-banks
Items.Abstract: Line Intensity Mapping has great promise to allow us deeper insight and provide better constraints into a variety of cosmological studies. To enable this technology, we need compact and high efficiency spectrometers that are scalable. One such spectrometer is the waveguide filter-bank. Here we present the design, fabrication, and optical testing of a silicon micromachined prototype at room and cryogenic temperatures. This device is designed in a split-block architecture and can be readily fabricated using silicon micromachining processes. Compared to the lossless design which has a maximum spectral efficiency of 0.5, the single-channel (260 GHz), gold-plated prototype was measured to have a maximum spectral efficiency over 0.38 with a resolving power of R = 263 when measured at room temperature and we discuss performance enhancements when operated at cryogenic temperatures. Multiple metallization schemes were tested and compared.

Items.Authors: Rosly Renil, Hugo Hamman, Christopher Schollar, Martin Slabber
Items.Title: Managing Data Life Cycle Policies & Streamlining Science Data Operations
Items.Abstract: A Data Lifecycle Management (DLM) process brings order and clarity to an observatory's data information. This structure makes it easier to achieve essential goals like keeping data secure and ensuring it’s readily accessible when needed.     This poster presents a DLM strategy used for SARAO science operations, current challenges faced and MeerKAT systems that focuses heavily on safeguarding data and enabling disaster recovery—especially important as cyber threats rise alongside the rapid expansion of digital information. By having a reliable recovery plan ready to go, observatories can reduce the financial damage and reputational harm caused by unexpected events.

Items.Authors: Runa Briguglio, Matteo Menessini, Marco Xompero, Ciro Del Vecchio, Daniele Gallieni, Matteo Tintori
Items.Title: Mass budget analysis for a contactless active mirror for space telescopes
Items.Abstract: Active mirrors are considered key components for future large aperture space telescopes such as the HWO. Recently, a technology based on contactless active mirrors, developed for ground based observatory, has been proposed and preliminary tested in the lab. In a contactless active mirror, the optical surface is a thin Zerodur glass shell controlled by voice coil actuators and monitored by capacitive sensors; as a result, the optical surface is mechanically decoupled from the support. Such point has relevant implications from a system-wise perspective, as the support structure has no optical specifications any longer: in particular, the support may be extremely light-weighted, while having little to no print-through on the optical surface. The concept has been preliminary demonstrated on a 40 cm diameter prototype with 19 actuators, featuring an areal density as low as 18 kg/m2. In this work we discuss the as-build mass budget and present a roadmap to further improve the mass budget.

Items.Authors: Anthony Soulain, Alexis Matter, Philippe Bério, Stéphane Lagarde, Romain Petrov, Florentin Millour, Bruno Lopez
Items.Title: MATISSE-py: a high-level python interface enabling efficient and automated data reduction for the VLTI/MATISSE
Items.Abstract: We present MATISSE-py, a Python package automating the complex reduction of VLTI/MATISSE interferometric data. It provides a modular abstraction layer over the official ESO pipeline, enabling scripted workflows, batch processing, and integration with modern data-analysis environments. We also introduce enhanced calibration algorithms - including refined BCD correction, robust transfer function handling, and v-factor computation - derived from seven years of operations, significantly improving data quality. Featuring robust quality control, interactive Plotly visualizations, and full compatibility with official binaries, MATISSE-py streamlines reduction for both experts and new users, paving the way for a modernized, reproducible reduction ecosystem.

Items.Authors: Elia Costa, Bernardo Salasnich, Andrea Baruffolo, Mirko Colapietro, Fabio Rossi, Daniela Fantinel, Salvatore Savarese
Items.Title: MAVIS Instrument Control Software System: Post-FDR Update and Redesign of the Interface with the Two PFDMs
Items.Abstract: MAVIS (Multi-conjugate Adaptive optics Visible Imager and Spectrograph) is a next-generation adaptive optics instrument designed for the VLT AOF, and its Instrument Control Software System (ICSS) plays a key role in its operation. This paper presents the current design of the MAVIS ICSS following a successful Final Design Review (FDR) in October 2025. The ICSS has undergone a critical update that includes the complete redesign of the interface with the two Post-Focal Deformable Mirrors (PFDMs). This new interface has been seamlessly integrated within the ESO Instrument Software Framework (IFW). A key architectural change involves moving the complexity of the PFDM interaction to the Programmable Logic Controller (PLC), where the actual control logic is implemented. Besides the monitoring, the ICSS allows for non-real-time control of the Deformable Mirrors (DM), a functionality highly useful during the Assembly, Integration and Test (AIT) phase.

Items.Authors: Paolo Cerpelloni, Luca Marafatto, Davide Greggio, Matteo Aliverti, Stefan Ströbele, Mirko Colapietro, Simone Doniselli, Kalyan Kumar Radhakrishnan Santhakumari, Oleksandra Rebrysh, Maria Bergomi, Valentina Viotto, François Rigaut
Items.Title: MAVIS: AIV procedures for the post focal relay
Items.Abstract: This paper presents the alignment concept, workflow, and tooling developed for the MAVIS PFR (Post Focal  Relay) Assembly, Integration and Verification phase at the Astronomical Observatory of Padova. We describe  the reference architecture, measurement strategy, error budget, and sequencing logic that enable alignment of  the entire PFR chain to the required tolerances, highlighting the advantages and constraints of this hybrid  mechanical–optical approach.

Items.Authors: Paolo Cerpelloni, Alessandro Ballone, Kalyan Kumar Radhakrishnan Santhakumari, Davide Greggio, Luca Marafatto, Matteo Aliverti, Oleksandra Rebrysh, Daniele Vassallo, Gabriele Umbriaco, Elena Carolo, Remon van Gaalen, Lorenzo Merli, Maria Bergomi, Valentina Viotto, François Rigaut
Items.Title: MAVIS: diagnostic and NCPA Unit and laboratory verification
Items.Abstract: MAVIS Diagnostic and NCPA Unit (DNU) consists of two identical CMOS cameras mounted on a common linear stage. While the first camera allows for the on-axis pupil imaging mode, the second one, equipped with a multi-lenslet array, enables for the on-axis wavefront sensing mode. Although not planned to be used during night operations, the DNU wavefront sensing mode may be useful during the initial nighttime commissioning to measure on-axis residual aberrations and wavefront error in the entire light path with and without Multi-Conjugate Adaptive Optics loop running. In this proceeding, we describe the MAVIS DNU component, its functionalities, and its laboratory verification.

Items.Authors: Anthony J. Horton, Andrea Bianco, David Brodrick, Jennifer Burgess, David Clarke, Timothy Chin, Elia Costa, Mark Downing, Simon Ellis, Nuwanthika Fernando, Michele Frangiamore, Gaston Gausachs, Miguel Gonzalez Bolivar, Davide Greggio, Max Hewlett, Johan Kosmalski, Summer Luo, Nuria Lorente, Richard McDermid, Helen McGregor, Trevor Mendel, Brent Miszalski, Jonathan Moller, Tristan Monnier, Francois Rigaut, David Robertson, Bernardo Salasnich, Warrick Schofield, Dylan Simpfendorfer, Scott Smedley, Annino Vaccarella, Lew Waller, Ross Zhelem, Jessica Zheng
Items.Title: MAVIS: science instruments final design
Items.Abstract: The MAVIS Adaptive Optics Module, working together with the Adaptive Optics Facility of VLT Unit Telescope 4, will deliver a diffraction limited field 30 arcseconds in diameter at visible wavelengths. This will enable an unprecedented combination of spatial resolution, sensitivity and field of view, opening up new regions of parameter space for scientific exploration. To capitalise on this capability MAVIS needs two scientific instruments; a multi-band imager covering the full 30 arcsecond corrected field while sampling the diffraction limited PSF, and an integral field spectrograph covering the full range of visible wavelengths. In this paper we describe the design of the MAVIS Imager and Spectrograph as presented at the recent MAVIS Final Design Review, and discuss some of the challenges, trade offs, and processes which led us to these designs.
